cards.title: 1.1 Refraction of Light at an Interface
body: The bending or change in the direction of propagation of light as it passes from one medium to another is known as **refraction**.
The ray of light which travels into the second medium is called the **refracted ray**.
The point at which the incident ray strikes the surface of separation of the two media is called the **point of incidence**.
The perpendicular line drawn to the surface of separation at the point of incidence is called the **normal**.
As light passes from a vacuum to another medium it slows down.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: An underwater object is viewed from directly above in air. If the actual depth of the object is $$4.00 \text{ m}$$, what is its apparent depth? (Refractive index of water = $$1.33$$)
cards.why:
**Step 1: State the given values**
$$\text{Real Depth} = 4.00 \text{ m}$$
$$n = 1.33$$

**Step 2: State the formula**
$$n = \frac{\text{Real Depth}}{\text{Apparent Depth}} \implies \text{Apparent Depth} = \frac{\text{Real Depth}}{n}$$

**Step 3: Substitute and solve**
$$\text{Apparent Depth} = \frac{4.00 \text{ m}}{1.33} \approx 3.0075 \text{ m}$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The apparent depth of the object is **$$3.01 \text{ m}$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the critical angle for light travelling from water ($$n = 1.33$$) into air ($$n = 1.00$$)?
cards.why:
**Step 1: State the given values**
$$n_1 = 1.33 \text{ (denser medium)}$$
$$n_2 = 1.00 \text{ (rarer medium)}$$

**Step 2: State the critical angle formula**
$$\sin \theta_c = \frac{n_2}{n_1}$$

**Step 3: Substitute and calculate**
$$\sin \theta_c = \frac{1.00}{1.33} \approx 0.7519$$
$$\theta_c = \sin^{-1}(0.7519) \approx 48.75^\circ$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The critical angle is **$$48.8^\circ$$**.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand the physical mechanism of refraction**
Refraction is defined as the bending of light when it transitions from one medium to another. This occurs because the speed (phase velocity) of light changes due to the different optical densities of the media.

**Step 2: Eliminate incorrect options**
The frequency of a wave is determined by the source and remains constant across boundaries. Amplitude and absorption do not cause the geometric bending of the wave propagation direction.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the primary cause is the **change in the phase velocity of the light wave**.

cards.title: 1.1 Refraction of Light, Snell's Law, and Apparent Depth (1/4)
body: **Refraction** is the bending or change in direction of propagation of a light wave as it passes from one transparent medium to another of different optical density, caused by a change in its phase velocity.

When a wave transitions between media, its frequency remains strictly constant because it is determined solely by the source of the oscillation. However, because the phase velocity of light is slower in optically denser media (where the refractive index $$n > 1$$), the wavelength must decrease proportionally according to the wave relationship $$v = f \lambda$$. This spatial compression of wavefronts at an oblique boundary causes the wave direction to pivot toward the normal when entering a denser medium, and away from the normal when entering a rarer medium.

To visualize this, consider the classic lawnmower analogy: when a lawnmower rolls at an angle from smooth pavement onto thick grass, the wheel that enters the grass first slows down immediately while the other wheel continues at high speed on the pavement. This speed mismatch forces the entire lawnmower to pivot, changing its trajectory. In optics, the degree of this bending is quantified by the absolute refractive index $$n$$, defined as the dimensionless ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum $$c$$ to its speed in the medium $$v$$:
$$n = \frac{c}{v}$$

cards.title: 1.1 Refraction of Light, Snell's Law, and Apparent Depth (2/4)
body: At any planar interface between two media, this refraction is governed by Snell's Law. Mathematically, it states that the product of the refractive index and the sine of the angle of incidence is constant across the interface:
$$n_1 \sin \theta_1 = n_2 \sin \theta_2$$
Here, the angles $$\theta_1$$ and $$\theta_2$$ are always measured relative to the normal, which is an imaginary perpendicular line constructed at the exact point of incidence.

Refraction yields several profound observational phenomena. For instance, when looking down into a body of water, light rays departing an underwater object bend away from the normal as they cross the boundary into the air. When these diverging rays reach the human eye, the brain traces them backward along straight lines, projecting a virtual image that is shallower than the physical object. This discrepancy is described by the relation:
$$n = \frac{\text{Real Depth}}{\text{Apparent Depth}}$$

cards.title: 1.1 Refraction of Light, Snell's Law, and Apparent Depth (3/4)
body: Furthermore, when light attempts to travel from an optically denser medium to a rarer medium (such as from glass to air), there exists a unique angle of incidence called the **Critical Angle** ($$\theta_c$$) at which the angle of refraction is exactly $$90^\circ$$. At this point, the refracted ray skims along the interface. This angle is calculated by:
$$\theta_c = \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{n_2}{n_1}\right)$$

If the angle of incidence exceeds $$\theta_c$$, the light cannot refract into the second medium at all. Instead, it is entirely reflected back into the denser medium. This phenomenon is known as **Total Internal Reflection** (TIR) and is the foundation of fiber-optic communication and the brilliance of cut diamonds.

cards.title: 1.1 Refraction of Light, Snell's Law, and Apparent Depth (4/4)
body: In non-uniform media, such as atmospheric air with temperature gradients, the refractive index varies continuously. On hot summer days, the air directly above asphalt is heated, making it less dense than the cooler air above it. Light rays from the sky bend progressively upward as they travel through these thermal layers, eventually undergoing total internal reflection near the road surface. This causes an optical illusion known as a **Mirage**, where the observer perceives a shimmering, wet surface reflecting the sky.

Substance — Refractive Index ($$n$$) — Speed of Light ($$v$$ in $$\text{m/s}$$) | Vacuum — $$1.0000$$ — $$3.00 \times 10^8$$ | Air — $$1.0003$$ — $$2.99 \times 10^8$$ | Water — $$1.3300$$ — $$2.26 \times 10^8$$ | Crown Glass — $$1.5200$$ — $$1.97 \times 10^8$$ | Diamond — $$2.4200$$ — $$1.24 \times 10^8$$

> **💡 Did You Know?**: Even though diamond has a very high refractive index ($$2.42$$), its sparkling brilliance is not just due to the material itself, but also to the precise geometric angles of its cut, which maximize total internal reflection.

> **🧠 Pro-Tip**: When solving Apparent Depth problems, remember that the formula $$n = \frac{\text{Real Depth}}{\text{Apparent Depth}}$$ assumes the observer is looking nearly straight down (normal viewing). For steep angles, the simple linear relationship breaks down due to trigonometric variations.

cards.title: What actually changes at a boundary
body: The source fixes **frequency**. Entering a denser medium, both speed and wavelength fall by the factor n. Colour stays the same idea in school language because f is unchanged. Only v and λ jump.
Quote the two refraction laws: rays and normal in one plane; sin i / sin r constant for two given media and one colour. “Optically denser” means larger n — not necessarily heavier liquid.

cards.title: TIR — all three must be true
body:
1. Light is already in the optically denser medium.
2. It is heading toward a rarer medium.
3. i > C with sin C = n_rarer / n_denser.

Fibre optics, diamond sparkle, binocular prisms and some mirages are TIR stories. A pool looks shallow because rays leaving water bend away from the normal and the brain extrapolates them straight — a raised virtual image.

cards.title: 1.2 Thin Lenses: Ray Diagrams, Lens Equation, and Power (1/4)
body: A **lens** is a transmissive optical device that focuses or disperses a light beam by means of refraction, characterized by curved surfaces that shape wavefronts.

Lenses are broadly categorized into two structural classes based on their cross-sectional profiles. A **converging lens** (or convex lens) is thicker at its center than at its edges and causes parallel incident rays to converge toward a real focus point. Conversely, a **diverging lens** (or concave lens) is thinner at its center than at its margins, causing parallel rays to diverge as if originating from a virtual focus point located behind the lens.

To analyze thin lenses, we define several critical terms. The *Principal Axis* is the horizontal line passing through the geometric centers of the lens's curved surfaces. The *Optical Center* ($$O$$) is the exact midpoint of the lens; any ray passing through $$O$$ undergoes negligible deviation. The *Principal Focus* or *Focal Point* ($$F$$) is the point where parallel rays converge (for convex lenses) or appear to diverge from (for concave lenses). The distance from the optical center to the focal point is the *Focal Length* ($$f$$).

Geometric ray tracing is a powerful visual tool used to predict image characteristics. By drawing three distinct principal rays from the top of an object, we can locate its image: 1. **The Parallel Ray**: Travels parallel to the principal axis and refracts through the focal point on the opposite side (for convex) or aligns with the virtual focus on the same side (for concave). 2. **The Central Ray**: Passes straight through the optical center $$O$$ without any angular deviation. 3. **The Focal Ray**: Passes through the focal point before reaching the lens and refracts parallel to the principal axis.

cards.title: 1.2 Thin Lenses: Ray Diagrams, Lens Equation, and Power (2/4)
body: For mathematical precision, we employ the Thin Lens Equation, which relates the object distance ($$d_o$$), image distance ($$d_i$$), and focal length ($$f$$):
The size and orientation of the image are governed by the linear magnification equation:
$$m = -\frac{d_i}{d_o} = \frac{h_i}{h_o}$$

cards.title: 1.2 Thin Lenses: Ray Diagrams, Lens Equation, and Power (3/4)
body: To ensure consistency, we strictly adhere to the real-is-positive sign convention: focal length $$f$$ is positive for converging lenses and negative for diverging lenses; object distance $$d_o$$ is always positive for real objects; image distance $$d_i$$ is positive for real images (formed on the opposite side of the lens) and negative for virtual images (formed on the same side as the object).
Another essential property of a lens is its refracting strength, known as **Optical Power** ($$P$$). It is defined as the reciprocal of its focal length measured in meters:

The SI unit of power is the **dioptre** ($$\text{D}$$, where $$1 \text{ D} = 1 \text{ m}^{-1}$$). Converging lenses have positive powers, while diverging lenses have negative powers. When multiple thin lenses are placed in close contact, their net optical power is simply the algebraic sum of their individual powers:
$$P_{\text{net}} = P_1 + P_2 + P_3 + \dots$$

cards.title: 1.2 Thin Lenses: Ray Diagrams, Lens Equation, and Power (4/4)
body: Lens Type — Focal Length ($$f$$) — Image Type — Sign of Power ($$P$$) | Converging (Convex) — Positive ($$+f$$) — Real (mostly) or Virtual — Positive ($$+P$$) | Diverging (Concave) — Negative ($$-f$$) — Virtual (always) — Negative ($$-P$$)

> **💡 Did You Know?**: When an object is placed exactly at twice the focal length ($$2f$$) of a converging lens, the resulting image is real, inverted, and exactly the same size as the object, located at $$2f$$ on the opposite side.
> **🧠 Pro-Tip**: If the magnification $$m$$ of a system is negative, the image is inverted and real. If $$m$$ is positive, the image is erect and virtual.

**Step 2: Identify the primary color combinations**

cards.title: 1.3 Optical Instruments
body: A basic compound microscope consists of two converging lenses.
The lens closest to the object is called the objective lens and the other lens closest to the eye is called **eyepiece lens**.
The focal length of the eyepiece is larger than the focal length of the objective.
The focal lengths of the objective and eyepiece lenses are 4.5 mm and 10 mm respectively.
The distance between the two lenses is adjusted to 25 mm.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following best describes the image formed by a diverging lens for any real object?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Recall the optical behavior of a diverging lens**
A diverging (concave) lens always spreads out incident light rays. The refracted rays never converge physically on the opposite side of the lens.

**Step 2: Analyze ray intersections**
Because the rays diverge, they only intersect when traced backward as virtual lines on the same side of the lens as the object. This guarantees that the image is always virtual, upright (erect), and smaller (diminished).

**Step 3: Final Result**
Thus, the image is always **Virtual, erect, diminished**.

cards.title: 1.3 Optical Instruments, the Human Eye, and Dispersion of Light (1/3)
body: An **optical instrument** is a device consisting of lenses, mirrors, or prisms designed to process light waves to enhance images for viewing or analysis.

The simplest optical instrument is the **Magnifying Glass**, which consists of a single converging lens. When an object is placed inside the focal point ($$d_o < f$$), the lens produces an enlarged, virtual, and erect image on the same side of the lens. To achieve greater magnification without extreme lens curvature, we use a **Compound Microscope**. This instrument utilizes two converging lenses: the *objective lens* (short focal length) and the *eyepiece lens* (longer focal length). The objective lens forms a real, inverted, and magnified intermediate image, which is then further magnified by the eyepiece to create a highly enlarged virtual final image.

Similarly, a **Refracting Telescope** is designed to view highly distant objects. It also consists of an objective and an eyepiece, but the objective lens has a very long focal length to capture distant parallel rays and form an intermediate image at its focal plane, which is then magnified by the eyepiece. The overall angular magnification of a telescope is given by:
$$m = -\frac{f_o}{f_e}$$

cards.title: 1.3 Optical Instruments, the Human Eye, and Dispersion of Light (2/3)
body: The **Human Eye** behaves as a natural optical instrument. Light entering the eye is refracted by the cornea and focused by the crystalline lens onto the light-sensitive retina. The eye adjusts its focus for varying distances by using the ciliary muscles to alter the curvature (and thus the focal length) of the lens, a process called **Accommodation**. The nearest point at which the eye can focus clearly without strain is the *Near Point* (typically $$25 \text{ cm}$$ for young adults).

When the accommodation mechanism fails, vision defects arise: 1. **Myopia** (Short-sightedness): The eyeball is too long or the lens is too curved, focusing distant light in front of the retina. This is corrected using a diverging (concave) lens. 2. **Hypermetropia** (Long-sightedness): The eyeball is too short or the lens is too flat, focusing near light behind the retina. This is corrected using a converging (convex) lens. 3. **Astigmatism**: The cornea has an irregular curvature, causing light to focus unevenly. This is corrected using a cylindrical lens.

Additionally, when white light passes through a glass prism, it undergoes **Dispersion**. This splitting of light into its component colors (the spectrum) occurs because different wavelengths of light travel at different speeds in glass. The shorter the wavelength, the more the light slows down and bends. Consequently, violet light (shortest visible wavelength) refracts the most, while red light (longest visible wavelength) refracts the least. This wavelength-dependent variation in refractive index is the primary cause of rainbows.

Instrument / System — Objective Lens — Eyepiece Lens — Final Image Characteristics | Microscope — Short $$f$$ — Long $$f$$ — Virtual, Inverted, Highly Magnified | Telescope — Long $$f$$ — Short $$f$$ — Virtual, Inverted, Magnified | Human Eye — Natural crystalline lens — None — Real, Inverted, Diminished (on retina)

cards.title: 1.3 Optical Instruments, the Human Eye, and Dispersion of Light (3/3)
body: > **💡 Did You Know?**: The human brain automatically flips the inverted real image formed on our retina, allowing us to perceive the world right-side up without any conscious effort.
> **🧠 Pro-Tip**: Remember that in a compound microscope, the intermediate image must fall just inside the focal point of the eyepiece lens to allow the eyepiece to act as a simple magnifier.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A mirage is primarily caused by which of the following optical phenomena?

options.A: Dispersion of light through hot air
options.B: Diffraction of light around dust particles
options.C: Atmospheric refraction due to temperature gradients
options.D: Polarization of sky light near the ground

cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand how mirages form**
A mirage is an optical illusion that occurs when there is a rapid temperature gradient in the air near the ground. Hot air near the ground has a lower density and a lower refractive index than the cooler air above it.

**Step 2: Trace light ray behavior**
Light rays from the sky bend progressively upward as they travel through these atmospheric layers with varying refractive indices. This bending is refraction. Near the ground, the angle of incidence eventually exceeds the critical angle, resulting in total internal reflection.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, a mirage is caused by **atmospheric refraction due to temperature gradients**.

cards.title: 1.4 Dispersion of Light
body: Colours are different types of light, recognised by their own wavelengths or frequencies.
Observations show that when a beam of white light passes through a glass prism the emerging light splits into a series of colours very much like a rain bow.
The resulting band of colours is called a **spectrum**.
The splitting of light into different colours is called **dispersion**.
The different speeds cause the different colours to be refracted by different amounts.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: An object is placed $$30.0 \text{ cm}$$ in front of a thin converging lens with a focal length of $$10.0 \text{ cm}$$. Where is the image located?

options.A: $$15.0 \text{ cm}$$ on the opposite side of the lens
options.B: $$7.50 \text{ cm}$$ on the same side as the object
options.C: $$30.0 \text{ cm}$$ on the opposite side of the lens
options.D: $$10.0 \text{ cm}$$ on the same side as the object

cards.why:
**Step 1: State the given values**
$$d_o = 30.0 \text{ cm}$$
$$f = 10.0 \text{ cm}$$

**Step 2: Use the lens equation**
$$\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{d_o} + \frac{1}{d_i} \implies \frac{1}{d_i} = \frac{1}{f} - \frac{1}{d_o}$$

**Step 3: Substitute and calculate**
$$\frac{1}{d_i} = \frac{1}{10.0} - \frac{1}{30.0} = \frac{3 - 1}{30.0} = \frac{2}{30.0}$$
$$d_i = \frac{30.0}{2} = 15.0 \text{ cm}$$
Since $$d_i$$ is positive, the image is real and located on the opposite side of the lens.

**Step 4: Final Result**
The image is located at **$$15.0 \text{ cm}$$ on the opposite side of the lens**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: When white light passes through a glass prism, which spectral color suffers the greatest angle of deviation?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Define dispersion and deviation**
As white light passes through a prism, different colors are refracted by different amounts. The deviation angle is the angle between the incident ray and the emergent ray.

**Step 2: Compare refractive indices**
In optical glass, the refractive index is greater for shorter wavelengths. Because violet light has the shortest visible wavelength, glass has the highest refractive index for violet: 
$$n_{\text{violet}} > n_{\text{red}}$$

**Step 3: Apply Snell's Law**
A higher refractive index causes a greater change in direction, meaning violet light bends and deviates the most.

**Step 4: Final Result**
Thus, **Violet** light suffers the greatest angle of deviation.

cards.title: Dispersion of light
body: Dispersion is the splitting of white light into its component colours because different wavelengths refract by slightly different amounts in a medium such as glass.
In a triangular prism, violet typically bends more than red, producing a spectrum. Rainbow formation also involves refraction and dispersion in water droplets.
The refractive index of glass depends weakly on wavelength; that wavelength dependence is the microscopic reason for dispersion.
Chromatic aberration in lenses is an unwanted effect of dispersion: different colours focus at slightly different places.

cards.q: Which type of corrective lens is prescribed for a person suffering from Myopia (short-sightedness)?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand Myopia**
In a myopic eye, parallel rays from distant objects are focused in front of the retina because the eye system has too much converging power.

**Step 2: Choose corrective action**
To correct this, we need to diverge the incoming parallel rays slightly before they enter the eye so that the natural lens focuses them further back, directly on the retina.

**Step 3: Identify the lens type**
A diverging (concave) lens provides the necessary pre-divergence.

**Step 4: Final Result**
Therefore, a **diverging lens** is used.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In the additive color theory of light, what is the complementary color of red light?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Define complementary colors**
Two colors of light are complementary if, when mixed in equal intensities, they produce white light.

**Step 2: Recall primary and secondary additive colors**
The three primary colors of light are Red, Green, and Blue. White light is formed by: 
$$\text{Red} + \text{Green} + \text{Blue} = \text{White}$$

**Step 3: Analyze the red component**
Since Green + Blue = Cyan, then:
$$\text{Red} + \text{Cyan} = \text{White}$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
Thus, the complementary color of red light is **Cyan**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the relationship between the focal length ($$f$$) and the radius of curvature ($$R$$) of a thin spherical lens?

options.D: There is no fixed simple relationship like mirrors because it depends on the refractive index of the glass.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Distinguish between mirrors and lenses**
For spherical mirrors, the focal length is geometrically fixed as $$f = \frac{R}{2}$$.

**Step 2: Examine lens focal parameters**
For a thin spherical lens, the focal length depends not only on the radii of curvature of its two surfaces ($$R_1$$ and $$R_2$$) but also on the refractive index of the lens material ($$n$$) and the surrounding medium, as described by the Lensmaker's Equation:
$$\frac{1}{f} = (n - 1)\left(\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right)$$

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, **there is no fixed simple relationship like mirrors because it depends on the refractive index of the glass**.

cards.title: 2.1 Magnets, Magnetic Fields, and Electromagnetism (1/4)
body: **Magnetism** is a class of physical phenomena mediated by magnetic fields, originating from the motion of electric charges—specifically the spin and orbital motion of electrons—resulting in attractive or repulsive forces between objects.

At the subatomic level, every electron behaves as a microscopic magnetic dipole due to its intrinsic spin and its orbital revolution around the nucleus. In most materials, the magnetic orientations of these electrons point in random directions, canceling each other out. However, in **ferromagnetic** materials like iron, cobalt, and nickel, quantum-mechanical effects cause the magnetic dipoles of adjacent atoms to align parallel to one another. This alignment forms localized regions called *magnetic domains*. When an external magnetic field is applied, these domains rotate and merge, turning the material into a permanent or temporary magnet. In contrast, **paramagnetic** materials (like aluminum) show only weak domain alignment in external fields, while **diamagnetic** materials (like bismuth) weakly oppose external fields.

A magnet always possesses two distinct poles: a north-seeking pole (N) and a south-seeking pole (S). If you cut a bar magnet in half, you do not isolate the poles; instead, two new complete dipoles are created, as magnetic monopoles do not exist in nature. The space surrounding a magnet is occupied by a vector quantity called the **Magnetic Field** ($$\mathbf{B}$$), also termed *Magnetic Flux Density*. By convention, magnetic field lines emerge from the north pole, curve through space, and enter the south pole, forming continuous closed loops that never intersect.

Our planet itself is a giant magnet. The Earth's magnetic field, or geomagnetism, is generated by convective currents of molten iron and nickel in its outer core. Interestingly, the Earth's geographic North Pole corresponds to its magnetic south pole, which is why the north pole of a compass needle points toward geographic north. This magnetic field acts as a protective shield (the magnetosphere), redirecting harmful solar wind particles away from our atmosphere.

cards.title: 2.1 Magnets, Magnetic Fields, and Electromagnetism (2/4)
body: In 1820, Hans Christian Oersted discovered a direct connection between electricity and magnetism. He observed that an electric current flowing through a wire deflected a nearby compass needle. This demonstrated that moving charges generate their own magnetic fields. For a long, straight, current-carrying wire, the magnetic field lines form concentric circles around the conductor. The direction of these lines is determined by the **Right-Hand Grip Rule**: if you grasp the wire with your right hand so that your thumb points in the direction of the conventional current ($$I$$), your curled fingers point in the direction of the magnetic field vector ($$\mathbf{B}$$). The magnitude of this field at a perpendicular distance $$r$$ from the wire is governed by:
$$B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$$
where $$\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \text{ T}\cdot\text{m/A}$$ is the permeability of free space.

By winding a long wire into a tight coil of $$N$$ turns, we construct a **solenoid**. When an electric current passes through the solenoid, the individual magnetic fields of each loop add together, producing a strong, highly uniform magnetic field inside the coil that resembles the field of a bar magnet. The magnetic field strength inside a long solenoid is calculated by:
$$B = \mu_0 n I = \mu_0 \left(\frac{N}{L}\right) I$$

This setup is the foundation of **electromagnets**, which are essential for cranes, magnetic relays, electric bells, and speakers.

cards.title: 2.2 Magnetic Force on Charges and Conductors (1/5)
body: The **Lorentz Force** (specifically its magnetic component) is the force exerted on a charged particle moving through a magnetic field, mathematically perpendicular to both the particle's velocity vector and the magnetic field vector.

When a point charge $$q$$ moves with a velocity vector $$\mathbf{v}$$ through an external magnetic field $$\mathbf{B}$$, it experiences a magnetic force $$\mathbf{F}_M$$. The magnitude of this force is given by:
$$F_M = |q| v B \sin \theta$$

where $$\theta$$ is the angle between the velocity vector $$\mathbf{v}$$ and the magnetic field vector $$\mathbf{B}$$. If the charge moves parallel to the field lines ($$\theta = 0^\circ$$ or $$180^\circ$$), the magnetic force is zero. The force is maximized when the charge moves perpendicular to the field ($$\theta = 90^\circ$$). The direction of this force is determined by the **Right-Hand Rule (RHR-1)**: point the fingers of your flat right hand in the direction of the velocity vector $$\mathbf{v}$$, curl them toward the magnetic field vector $$\mathbf{B}$$, and your extended thumb will point in the direction of the force acting on a *positive* charge. If the charge is *negative* (like an electron), the force points in the opposite direction.

cards.title: 2.2 Magnetic Force on Charges and Conductors (2/5)
body: Because the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity vector, the work done by the magnetic field on the moving charge is exactly zero ($$W = \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{d} = 0$$). Consequently, a magnetic field can change the direction of a charged particle's motion but cannot alter its kinetic energy or speed. When a charged particle enters a uniform magnetic field perpendicularly ($$\theta = 90^\circ$$), the magnetic force acts as a constant centripetal force. This forces the particle to travel in a perfect circle of radius $$r$$:
$$F_C = F_M \implies \frac{m v^2}{r} = q v B \implies r = \frac{m v}{q B}$$
This principle of mass-to-charge ratio separation is used in mass spectrometers and particle accelerators.

This magnetic force also acts on bulk electric currents. A wire of length $$L$$ carrying a conventional current $$I$$ in a magnetic field $$\mathbf{B}$$ is subject to a collective magnetic force. This is the sum of the individual forces acting on all the moving charge carriers (drift electrons) inside the conductor. The magnitude of this macroscopic force is:
$$F_M = I L B \sin \theta$$

cards.title: 2.2 Magnetic Force on Charges and Conductors (3/5)
body: where $$\theta$$ is the angle between the current direction (along the wire) and the magnetic field lines. The direction of this force is also found using the right-hand rule: point your thumb in the direction of the current $$I$$, your fingers in the direction of the magnetic field $$\mathbf{B}$$, and your palm will push in the direction of the force.

When two long, parallel, current-carrying conductors are placed close to each other, they exert mutual magnetic forces. Wire 1 produces a magnetic field $$B_1 = \frac{\mu_0 I_1}{2\pi d}$$ at the position of Wire 2. Wire 2, carrying current $$I_2$$ in this field, experiences a magnetic force. By combining these relationships, we find that the mutual force per unit length ($$F/L$$) between the two wires is:
$$\frac{F}{L} = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}$$

cards.title: 2.2 Magnetic Force on Charges and Conductors (4/5)
body: Using the right-hand rules, we observe a fundamental rule: **parallel currents attract** each other, while **antiparallel currents repel** each other. This physical interaction defines the SI base unit of electric current, the **Ampere**.

This force on current-carrying conductors is used to convert electrical energy into mechanical energy in **DC Motors**. A rectangular coil of wire is suspended between the poles of a permanent magnet. When current flows through the coil, opposite forces act on its two parallel sides, generating a net torque that rotates the loop. To keep the coil rotating in the same direction, a **split-ring commutator** reverses the current direction twice per rotation as the coil passes through the vertical position.

Physical Case — Governing Equation — Force Direction Rule — Key Variables | Moving Charge — $$F_M = q v B \sin \theta$$ — RHR-1 (Inverted for $$-q$$) — $$q$$ (charge), $$v$$ (velocity), $$B$$ (field) | Current-Carrying Wire — $$F_M = I L B \sin \theta$$ — RHR (Thumb=$$I$$, Fingers=$$B$$, Palm=Force) — $$I$$ (current), $$L$$ (length), $$B$$ (field) | Parallel Conductors — $$\frac{F}{L} = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}$$ — Attract (same dir) / Repel (opp dir) — $$I_1, I_2$$ (currents), $$d$$ (separation)

> **💡 Did You Know?**: The standard definition of one Ampere is the constant current which, if maintained in two straight parallel conductors of infinite length, placed $$1 \text{ m}$$ apart in a vacuum, produces a mutual force of exactly $$2 \times 10^{-7} \text{ N}$$ per meter of length.

cards.title: 2.3 Electromagnetic Induction, Generators, and Transformers (1/4)
body: **Electromagnetic Induction** is the production of an electromotive force (EMF) across an electrical conductor in a changing magnetic field, first discovered by Michael Faraday and Joseph Henry.

To understand this phenomenon, we must first define **Magnetic Flux** ($$\Phi_B$$). Magnetic flux is a measure of the total magnetic field passing through a given surface area. Mathematically, it is the dot product of the magnetic field vector $$\mathbf{B}$$ and the area vector $$\mathbf{A}$$ (which is perpendicular to the surface of the area):
$$\Phi_B = B A \cos \theta$$

where $$\theta$$ is the angle between the magnetic field vector and the normal to the surface area. The SI unit of magnetic flux is the **Weber** ($$\text{Wb}$$, where $$1 \text{ Wb} = 1 \text{ T}\cdot\text{m}^2$$). If the field lines are perpendicular to the surface area ($$\theta = 0^\circ$$), the flux is maximized ($$\Phi_B = BA$$); if the field lines run parallel to the surface area ($$\theta = 90^\circ$$), no lines pierce the surface, and the flux is zero.

cards.title: 2.3 Electromagnetic Induction, Generators, and Transformers (2/4)
body: Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction states that the magnitude of the induced EMF ($$\mathcal{E}$$) in a closed circuit is directly proportional to the time rate of change of the magnetic flux through the loop. For a coil consisting of $$N$$ turns, the law is written as:
$$\mathcal{E} = -N \frac{\Delta \Phi_B}{\Delta t}$$

The negative sign in this equation is not just a mathematical placeholder; it represents **Lenz's Law**. Lenz's Law states that the polarity of an induced EMF is always such that it generates a current whose own magnetic field opposes the change in the original magnetic flux that produced it. This law is a direct consequence of the *Conservation of Energy*. If the induced field reinforced the flux change, the magnetic flux would increase infinitely, creating energy out of nothing and violating the first law of thermodynamics.

When a solid piece of metal moves through a magnetic field, the changing flux induces circulating loops of current within the bulk metal. These are called **Eddy Currents**. According to Lenz's law, these circulating currents generate magnetic fields that oppose the motion of the metal, creating a strong magnetic drag. This effect is used in electromagnetic braking systems. However, in devices like transformers and AC motors, eddy currents are highly undesirable because they cause significant energy loss through Joule heating ($$I^2 R$$). To minimize these losses, transformer cores are constructed from thin sheets of iron insulated from one another, a design called a **laminated core**.

cards.title: 2.3 Electromagnetic Induction, Generators, and Transformers (3/4)
body: Electromagnetic induction is used to generate large-scale electricity in **Electric Generators**. An AC Generator consists of a loop of wire rotated mechanically inside a strong magnetic field. As the loop rotates, the angle $$\theta$$ changes continuously, causing the magnetic flux to vary sinusoidally. This generates an alternating EMF. The maximum EMF produced by a generator with $$N$$ turns of area $$A$$ rotating at an angular frequency $$\omega = 2\pi f$$ in a magnetic field $$B$$ is:
$$\mathcal{E}_{\text{max}} = N B A \omega = N B A (2\pi f)$$

Another essential application of induction is the **Transformer**, which increases or decreases AC voltages. It consists of two separate coils—the primary coil ($$N_p$$ turns) and the secondary coil ($$N_s$$ turns)—wound around a shared laminated iron core. When an alternating voltage ($$V_p$$) is applied to the primary coil, it creates a continuously changing magnetic flux in the core, which induces an alternating voltage ($$V_s$$) in the secondary coil. The relationship between these voltages is given by the transformer equation:
$$\frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{N_s}{N_p} = \frac{I_p}{I_s}$$

cards.title: 2.3 Electromagnetic Induction, Generators, and Transformers (4/4)
body: If $$N_s > N_p$$, the output voltage is increased, creating a **step-up transformer**. If $$N_s < N_p$$, it is a **step-down transformer**. Due to the conservation of energy, an ideal transformer cannot increase power; therefore, stepping up the voltage proportionally steps down the current.

Device / Component — Operational Principle — Primary Energy Transfer — Key Design Features | AC Generator — Rotational flux change — Mechanical to Electrical — Slip-rings and brushes | DC Generator — Rotational flux change with commutator — Mechanical to Pulsating DC — Split-ring commutator | Transformer — Mutual induction between coils — Electrical (AC) to Electrical — Laminated soft-iron core

> **💡 Did You Know?**: Power grids transmit electricity over long distances at incredibly high voltages (up to $$500,000 \text{ V}$$) and low currents. This minimizes energy loss due to heating in transmission wires, as power loss is proportional to the square of the current ($$P_{\text{loss}} = I^2 R$$).

> **🧠 Pro-Tip**: Transformers strictly require alternating current (AC) to operate. If you connect a transformer's primary winding to a direct current (DC) battery, the constant current will produce a constant magnetic field, the change in flux ($$\Delta \Phi_B / \Delta t$$) will be zero, and no voltage will be induced in the secondary coil.

cards.title: 3.1 Fundamental Wave Mechanics and Wave Behaviors (1/4)
body: A **wave** is a repeating disturbance or oscillation that travels through space-time, accompanied by a transfer of energy from one point to another without the permanent physical transport of matter.

Waves are categorized into two fundamental classes based on their propagation mechanisms: mechanical and electromagnetic. **Mechanical waves** require a physical medium (such as a solid, liquid, or gas) to travel. Examples include water ripples, slinky waves, and sound. These waves propagate because adjacent particles within the medium collide, transferring kinetic energy from one particle to the next. In contrast, **electromagnetic waves** (including visible light, radio waves, and X-rays) do not require a material medium. They consist of mutually perpendicular electric and magnetic field oscillations and propagate through empty space at the speed of light, $$c \approx 3.00 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}$$.

Additionally, waves are classified by the direction of particle oscillation relative to the direction of wave propagation. In a **transverse wave**, the particles of the medium oscillate perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of energy transport. Light, waves on a vibrating string, and surface water waves are prime examples. In a **longitudinal wave**, the particles of the medium oscillate parallel to the direction of energy transport, creating alternating regions of high density (**compressions**) and low density (**rarefactions**). Sound waves are the most common longitudinal waves.

To analyze wave motion mathematically, we define several critical parameters. The *amplitude* ($$A$$) is the maximum displacement of a particle from its equilibrium position. The *wavelength* ($$\lambda$$) is the distance between any two adjacent in-phase points, such as successive crests in a transverse wave or successive compressions in a longitudinal wave. The *frequency* ($$f$$) is the number of complete wave cycles that pass a given point in one second, measured in Hertz ($$\text{Hz}$$, where $$1 \text{ Hz} = 1 \text{ s}^{-1}$$). The *period* ($$T$$) is the time required for one complete wave cycle to pass a fixed point, which is the reciprocal of frequency:

cards.title: 3.2 Sound Waves: Production, Speed, and Behavior (1/3)
body: **Sound** is a mechanical, longitudinal wave produced by vibrating objects, propagating through a compressible medium (solid, liquid, or gas) via a series of alternating high-pressure regions (compressions) and low-pressure regions (rarefactions).

All sounds originate from vibrating matter. For instance, when you speak, your vocal cords vibrate, forcing surrounding air molecules to oscillate. Because sound is a mechanical wave, it requires a material medium to travel. It cannot propagate through a vacuum because there are no particles to transmit collisions. This is demonstrated by the classic bell jar experiment: as air is pumped out of a jar containing a ringing electric bell, the sound becomes progressively fainter until it dies away completely, even though the hammer can still be seen striking the bell.

Sound travels at different speeds depending on the physical properties of the medium, specifically its elasticity (bulk modulus) and density. Sound travels fastest in solids because their closely packed, highly elastic atomic bonds transfer kinetic energy rapidly. It travels slower in liquids and slowest in gases, where molecules are far apart and collisions are less frequent. For example, at $$25^\circ\text{C}$$, sound travels at approximately $$347 \text{ m/s}$$ in air, $$1498 \text{ m/s}$$ in water, and $$4877 \text{ m/s}$$ in aluminum.

In a gas like air, the speed of sound is highly dependent on temperature. As air temperature increases, its molecules move faster and collide more frequently, which increases the speed of sound. This relationship is given by the linear expression:

Additionally, sound waves are classified by frequency relative to human hearing limits: 1. **Audible Range**: Frequencies between $$20 \text{ Hz}$$ and $$20,000 \text{ Hz}$$ (approximately) that can be detected by the human ear. This range decreases with age due to natural wear and tear of sensory cells in the inner ear. 2. **Infrasound**: Frequencies below $$20 \text{ Hz}$$. Sources of infrasound include earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and heavy industrial machinery. Some animals, such as elephants, use infrasound to communicate over long distances. 3. **Ultrasound**: Frequencies above $$20,000 \text{ Hz}$$. Ultrasound is used extensively in medicine for internal imaging (sonography), in industry to find internal flaws in metal castings, and by animals like bats and dolphins for echolocation and navigation.

When a sound wave strikes a hard surface, it is reflected. This reflected sound wave is called an **echo**. Because the human brain retains a sound sensation for about $$0.1 \text{ s}$$ (persistence of hearing), the reflected sound must arrive at least $$0.1 \text{ s}$$ after the original sound to be perceived as a distinct echo. At room temperature, this requires the reflecting surface to be at least $$17 \text{ m}$$ away from the source. In smaller rooms, multiple overlapping reflections occur within $$0.1 \text{ s}$$, merging into a continuous, decaying sound called **reverberation**. If two sound sources with slightly different frequencies ($$f_1$$ and $$f_2$$) are played together, they interfere to produce periodic fluctuations in loudness called **beats**. The number of beats heard per second is the *beat frequency* ($$f_b$$):

cards.title: 3.3 Acoustics (Intensity, Pitch, and Quality) and Electromagnetic Waves (1/3)
body: **Acoustics** is the interdisciplinary science that deals with the study of mechanical waves in gases, liquids, and solids—including vibration, sound, ultrasound, and infrasound—characterized perceptually by intensity, pitch, and quality.
**Sound Intensity** ($$I$$) is defined as the power ($$P$$) carried by sound waves per unit area ($$A$$) perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation:
$$I = \frac{\text{Power}}{\text{Area}} = \frac{P}{A}$$

The SI unit of intensity is watts per square meter ($$\text{W/m}^2$$). The human ear has an incredibly wide range of sensitivity, detecting sound intensities from $$10^{-12} \text{ W/m}^2$$ (the *threshold of hearing*, $$I_0$$) up to $$1 \text{ W/m}^2$$ (the *threshold of pain*). Due to this exponential range, we measure sound intensity levels ($$\beta$$) on a logarithmic scale in **decibels** ($$\text{dB}$$):
$$\beta = 10 \log_{10}\left(\frac{I}{I_0}\right)$$

body: where $$I_0 = 1.00 \times 10^{-12} \text{ W/m}^2$$. An increase in intensity by a factor of $$10$$ corresponds to a level increase of $$10 \text{ dB}$$. An increase by a factor of $$100$$ corresponds to an increase of $$20 \text{ dB}$$. While loudness is a subjective sensation, a $$10 \text{ dB}$$ increase is generally perceived by humans as a doubling of loudness.

Additionally, we describe sound using several subjective properties and their physical counterparts: 1. **Pitch**: The subjective perception of the frequency of a sound wave. A high-frequency wave is perceived as a high pitch (e.g., a flute), while a low-frequency wave is perceived as a low pitch (e.g., a bass drum). 2. **Loudness**: The subjective perception of the amplitude and intensity of the sound wave. 3. **Quality (Timbre)**: The acoustic character that allows us to distinguish between two sounds of the same pitch and loudness produced by different sources (such as a violin and a piano). This distinct quality is determined by the specific blend of **harmonics** (integer multiples of the fundamental frequency, $$f_1, 2f_1, 3f_1, \dots$$) and **overtones** present in the sound wave.

In addition to acoustics, this unit covers **Electromagnetic (EM) Waves**. Unlike sound, EM waves are transverse, non-mechanical waves that travel through a vacuum. They are produced by accelerating charged particles, such as vibrating electrons within atoms. The electric ($$\mathbf{E}$$) and magnetic ($$\mathbf{B}$$) fields in an EM wave oscillate perpendicular to each other and to the direction of wave propagation.

All EM waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum ($$c = 3.00 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}$$). Because EM waves are transverse, they can be **polarized**. Polarization is the process of restricting the oscillations of the electric field vector to a single plane of vibration, a property that is impossible for longitudinal waves like sound.

Human hearing roughly spans about $$20\text{ Hz}$$ to $$20\text{ kHz}$$, with sensitivity best in the middle of that range.

cards.title: 3.6 Musical Sound and Noise
body: **Music** is a group of sounds that have been deliberately produced to make a regular pattern.
Certain combinations of tones are pleasant to hear, while other combinations are not pleasant.
Musical instruments do not produce notes of one frequency only.
Generally noise is considered to be a combination of sounds of varying pitch, i.e., of irregular frequencies.

**Sometimes it** is a mere annoyance, but loud noise can cause loss of hearing, and this could be a problem particularly in factories and other industrial works, where the sound level may be high for long periods.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Match subjective properties to physical counterparts**
- Pitch is the subjective perception of the frequency of a sound wave. High frequency corresponds to high pitch; low frequency corresponds to low pitch.
- Loudness corresponds to amplitude and intensity.

**Step 2: Final Result**
Therefore, pitch is determined by **Frequency**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Two waves of equal amplitude and frequency travel in the same medium. If they are exactly $$180.0^\circ$$ out of phase when they overlap, what happens?

options.A: They undergo complete constructive interference, doubling the amplitude.
options.B: They undergo complete destructive interference, resulting in zero amplitude.
options.C: They undergo refraction, changing their frequency.
options.D: They produce beats with a high frequency.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Apply the Principle of Superposition**
When two waves are $$180.0^\circ$$ out of phase, a crest of one wave aligns perfectly with a trough of the other wave.

**Step 2: Calculate the net displacement**
Since their amplitudes are equal but opposite, the sum of their displacements is exactly zero ($$A + (-A) = 0$$), representing complete destructive interference.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, **they undergo complete destructive interference, resulting in zero amplitude**.

Therefore, **they undergo complete destructive interference, resulting in zero amplitude**.

cards.title: Musical sound and noise
body: Musical sounds usually have regular, repeating waveforms and definite pitch. Noise is irregular and often has no clear pitch.
Instruments produce standing waves in strings, air columns or membranes; the allowed frequencies set the notes.
Noise pollution matters because high sound levels can damage hearing and affect concentration and health.
Beats occur when two close frequencies sound together, producing a throbbing loudness variation at the difference frequency.

cards.title: 3.7 Electromagnetic Waves
body: **Electromagnetic wave** is the name given to a whole range of transverse waves having different wavelengths but with common properties.
Electromagnetic waves have a wide range of wavelengths and frequencies.
The wide range of electromagnetic waves with different frequencies and wavelengths form the electromagnetic spectrum.
Even though electromagnetic waves have different names, they all travel at the speed of light in empty space.
Many of the electromagnetic spectrum regions overlap, the distinction between one region and another lying in the way in which radiations are produced.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A radio receiver is tuned to a station broadcasting at $$12.0 \text{ MHz}$$. What is the wavelength of this electromagnetic wave in a vacuum?
cards.why:
**Step 1: State given values**
$$f = 12.0 \text{ MHz} = 1.20 \times 10^7 \text{ Hz}$$
$$c = 3.00 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}$$

**Step 2: Formula**
$$\lambda = \frac{c}{f}$$

**Step 3: Substitution**
$$\lambda = \frac{3.00 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}}{1.20 \times 10^7 \text{ Hz}} = 25.0 \text{ m}$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The wavelength is **$$25.0 \text{ m}$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following optical characteristics uniquely distinguishes transverse waves from longitudinal waves?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Compare transverse and longitudinal behaviors**
- Both transverse and longitudinal waves can undergo reflection, refraction, diffraction, and interference.
- Only transverse waves can be polarized because polarization restricts oscillations to a single plane perpendicular to propagation. Longitudinal waves oscillate only along the single plane of propagation and cannot be restricted perpendicularly.

**Step 2: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct property is **Polarization**.

cards.title: Electromagnetic waves — overview
body: Electromagnetic (EM) waves are oscillating electric and magnetic fields that travel through space. In vacuum they move at $$c \approx 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}$$.
The EM spectrum includes radio, microwave, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays — same wave family, different frequency/wavelength.
Higher frequency means higher photon energy and usually greater penetration or ionizing ability (X-rays, gamma).
Visible light is only a thin band of the spectrum; radio waves have long wavelengths, gamma rays very short ones.

Sound travels through gases, liquids and solids.

λ = v/f, so the wavelength is larger in water.

questions.tip: f fixed, v and λ change together.

similar.q: A point source of sound emits sound waves uniformly in all directions. The intensity of sound at a distance of 50 cm from the source is 3.6 × 10⁻⁸ W/m². The intensity level of the sound at a distance 300 cm from the source is (take the intensity I₀ = 1.0 × 10⁻¹² W/m²)  A) 20 dB.  B) 30 dB.  C) 40 dB.  D) 50 dB.  E) 60 dB.
similar.a: B. 30 dB. — Intensity level β = 10 log(I/I₀) = 10 log(10⁻⁹/10⁻¹²) = 10 × 3 = 30 dB (G11 pp.201–205). Answer: B.

questions.q: Distinguish transverse and longitudinal waves in one line.
why: Transverse: particles vibrate perpendicular (⊥) to the direction of travel.
Longitudinal: particles vibrate parallel (∥) to the direction of travel.
Examples: light (transverse), sound (longitudinal).
questions.label: 9. Distinguish transverse and longitudinal waves in one line.
questions.tip: T for Transverse and "T-shape" (at right angles).

similar.q: The distance between a crest and an adjacent trough of a transverse wave of frequency 2,000 Hz is 40 cm. The speed of the wave, in m/s, is  A) 1,250.  B) 2,500.  C) 800.  D) 1,600.  E) 5,000.

questions.q: What type of wave is sound in air?
why: Air molecules vibrate back and forth along the direction the sound travels.
This makes compressions (high pressure) and rarefactions (low pressure).
So sound in air is longitudinal.
questions.label: 10. What type of wave is sound in air?
questions.tip: Gases cannot carry transverse waves.

similar.q: Light: which type?

questions.q: What type of wave is light?
why: Light consists of electric and magnetic fields oscillating.
The fields oscillate at right angles to the direction of travel.
So light is a transverse electromagnetic wave.
questions.label: 11. What type of wave is light?
questions.tip: Polarisation proves light is transverse.

similar.q: Does sound need a medium?

questions.q: Does sound need a medium?
why: Sound is a mechanical wave carried by vibrating particles, so it needs a medium.
Light is an EM wave made of fields, so it needs none.
Sound cannot cross a vacuum; light can.
questions.label: 12. Does sound need a medium?
questions.tip: In space, explosions are silent.

similar.q:
A sound of intensity level 60 dB has an intensity, in W/m², of
[I₀ = 10⁻¹² W/m²]  A) 10⁻⁸.  B) 10⁻⁶.  C) 10⁻⁵.  D) 10⁻².  E) 10⁻⁴.
similar.a: B. 10⁻⁶. — 60 = 10 log(I/10⁻¹²) → log(I/10⁻¹²) = 6 → I = 10⁶ × 10⁻¹² = 10⁻⁶ W/m². Answer: B.

questions.q: What is the approximate speed of sound in air?
questions.answer: 340 m/s at usual room conditions (use the value the paper gives).
why: The speed of sound in air depends on temperature.
At room temperature it is about 340 m/s (330 m/s at 0 °C).
In exams, use the value the question gives.
questions.label: 13. What is the approximate speed of sound in air?
questions.tip: Sound is about a million times slower than light.

similar.q: Echo t=0.40 s, v=340. d?

questions.q: An echo returns after 0.40 s (v = 340 m/s). How far away is the reflector?
why: d = vt/2 (the sound travels there and back).
questions.label: 14. An echo returns after 0.40 s (v = 340 m/s). How far away is the reflector?
questions.tip: Halve the round trip.

similar.q: d=255 m, v=340. Echo t?

questions.q: A reflector is 255 m away (v = 340 m/s). How long does the echo take?
why: The sound travels 2d: t = 2d/v.
questions.label: 15. A reflector is 255 m away (v = 340 m/s). How long does the echo take?
questions.tip: Distance doubles for an echo.

similar.q: Bat pulse, echo 0.020 s, v=340. Range?

questions.q: A bat's pulse returns after 0.020 s (v = 340 m/s). How far away is the insect?
why: d = vt/2.
questions.label: 16. A bat's pulse returns after 0.020 s (v = 340 m/s). How far away is the insect?
questions.tip: Bats use ultrasound echoes to find prey.

similar.q: Sound faster in steel than air. Why?
similar.a: Stronger coupling / higher modulus, particles closer.

questions.q: Why does sound travel faster in steel than in air?
questions.answer: Stronger coupling / higher modulus, particles closer.
why: Steel particles are closely packed and strongly bonded (high stiffness).
A disturbance is passed on very quickly from particle to particle.
In air the molecules are far apart, so the vibration passes more slowly.
questions.label: 17. Why does sound travel faster in steel than in air?
questions.tip: Put your ear to a rail – the sound arrives before the sound in air.

similar.q: How does the speed of sound compare in warm air and in cold air?

questions.q: How does the speed of sound compare in warm air and in cold air?
why: Sound speed in a gas increases with temperature.
Warmer molecules move faster and pass on the vibration sooner.
So sound is slightly faster in warm air.
questions.label: 18. How does the speed of sound compare in warm air and in cold air?
questions.tip: About +0.6 m/s for each 1 °C rise.

similar.q: Crest to next-but-one crest. Distance?

questions.q: What is the distance from one crest to the next-but-one crest?
why: Crest to the next crest = λ.
Next-but-one crest is two crests along.
Distance = 2λ.
questions.label: 19. What is the distance from one crest to the next-but-one crest?
questions.tip: Count the gaps between crests, not the crests.

similar.q: What is the distance from a compression to the adjacent rarefaction?

questions.q: What is the distance from a compression to the adjacent rarefaction?
why: Compression to compression = λ.
A rarefaction lies halfway between two compressions.
So compression to adjacent rarefaction = λ/2.
questions.label: 20. What is the distance from a compression to the adjacent rarefaction?
questions.tip: Like crest to trough on a transverse wave.

similar.q: Two points λ apart. Phase?

questions.q: Two points on a wave are one wavelength apart. What is their phase relation?
why: One wavelength apart means one whole cycle apart.
They are at the same stage of vibration.
So they are in phase.
questions.label: 21. Two points on a wave are one wavelength apart. What is their phase relation?
questions.tip: Whole numbers of λ → in phase.

similar.q: Two points λ/2 apart. Phase?

questions.q: Two points on a wave are λ/2 apart. What is their phase relation?
why: λ/2 is half a cycle.
One point is at a crest when the other is at a trough.
They are in antiphase (opposite phase).
questions.label: 22. Two points on a wave are λ/2 apart. What is their phase relation?
questions.tip: Odd multiples of λ/2 → antiphase.

similar.q: What determines the frequency of a wave?

questions.q: What determines the frequency of a wave?
why: The wave's frequency equals the frequency of the vibrating source.
Changing the medium changes v and λ, not f.
So the source determines the frequency.
questions.label: 23. What determines the frequency of a wave?
questions.tip: f is "born" at the source.

similar.q: Which wave property does loudness depend on?

questions.q: Which wave property does loudness depend on?
why: Loudness depends on how much energy arrives per second.
That depends on the amplitude (intensity ∝ A²).
So loudness depends on amplitude.
questions.label: 24. Which wave property does loudness depend on?
questions.tip: Bigger amplitude = louder.

similar.q: When a piano and then a flute play a note of the same loudness and the same pitch, there is a clear difference in the overall sound due to sound  A) pitch.  B) quality.  C) loudness.  D) note.  E) volume.
similar.a: B. quality. — Pitch depends on frequency and loudness on amplitude; both are the same here. The difference comes from the quality (timbre) of the sound – the different overtones (harmonics) mixed with the fundamental (G11 p.206–210). Answer: B.

questions.q: Which wave property does pitch depend on?
why: Pitch is how high a note sounds.
It depends on the number of vibrations per second.
So pitch depends on frequency.
questions.label: 25. Which wave property does pitch depend on?
questions.tip: Higher f = higher pitch.

similar.q: Radio λ=3.0 m. f?

questions.q: A radio wave has λ = 3.0 m. Find its frequency.
why: f = c/λ.
f = 1.0 × 10⁸ Hz = 100 MHz (FM radio).
questions.label: 26. A radio wave has λ = 3.0 m. Find its frequency.
questions.tip: 1 MHz = 10⁶ Hz.

similar.q: Microwave f=2.45 GHz. λ?

questions.q: A microwave has f = 2.45 GHz. Find its wavelength.
why: λ = c/f, with 2.45 GHz = 2.45 × 10⁹ Hz.
questions.label: 27. A microwave has f = 2.45 GHz. Find its wavelength.
questions.tip: Convert GHz to Hz (× 10⁹) first.

similar.q: Green 5.5×10^14 Hz. λ?

questions.q: Green 5.5×10^14 Hz. λ?
questions.label: 28. Green 5.5×10^14 Hz. λ?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: Put in order of increasing λ: X-rays, IR, green light, radio.

questions.q: Put in order of increasing λ: X-rays, IR, green light, radio.
why: Wavelength increases from gamma toward radio.
Of the four: X-rays (shortest), then green light, then infrared.
Radio has the longest wavelength: X → green → IR → radio.
questions.label: 29. Put in order of increasing λ: X-rays, IR, green light, radio.
questions.tip: Short λ = high f = high energy.

similar.q: Put the same list (X-rays, IR, green light, radio) in order of increasing f.

questions.q: Put the same list (X-rays, IR, green light, radio) in order of increasing f.
why: For EM waves f = c/λ, so the order of f is the reverse of the order of λ.
Radio has the lowest f, then IR, then green light.
X-rays have the highest: radio → IR → green → X.
questions.label: 30. Put the same list (X-rays, IR, green light, radio) in order of increasing f.
questions.tip: Reverse the wavelength order to get the frequency order.

similar.q: UV vs visible: danger?
similar.a: UV photons more energetic; can damage skin/eyes.

questions.q: UV vs visible: danger?
questions.answer: UV photons more energetic; can damage skin/eyes.
why: UV photons more energetic; can damage skin/eyes.
questions.label: 31. UV vs visible: danger?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: All EM in vacuum. Speed?

questions.q: At what speed do all EM waves travel in a vacuum?
why: All EM waves are the same kind of wave – electric and magnetic fields.
In a vacuum they all travel at the same speed.
questions.label: 32. At what speed do all EM waves travel in a vacuum?
questions.tip: Radio and gamma rays both travel at c.

similar.q: Water waves reflect off a wall. Law?
similar.a: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection.

questions.q: Water waves reflect off a straight wall. What law do they obey?
questions.answer: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection.
why: The wave hits the wall at an angle to the normal.
It bounces back at the same angle on the other side of the normal.
Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection.
questions.label: 33. Water waves reflect off a straight wall. What law do they obey?
questions.tip: Use a ripple tank to see this.

similar.q: 4 waves pass a post in 2.0 s. f?

questions.q: Four waves pass a post in 2.0 s. What is the frequency?
why: Frequency = number of waves ÷ time.
questions.label: 34. Four waves pass a post in 2.0 s. What is the frequency?
questions.tip: 1 Hz = 1 wave per second.

similar.q: Those waves have λ=1.2 m. v?

questions.q: Those waves (f = 2.0 Hz) have λ = 1.2 m. What is their speed?
why: v = fλ.
questions.label: 35. Those waves (f = 2.0 Hz) have λ = 1.2 m. What is their speed?
questions.tip: Hz × m = m/s.

similar.q: String 6.0 m holds 3 full waves. λ?

questions.q: A 6.0 m string holds exactly 3 full waves. What is the wavelength?
why: Length = number of waves × λ.
questions.label: 36. A 6.0 m string holds exactly 3 full waves. What is the wavelength?
questions.tip: Count full waves (crest + trough) carefully.

similar.q: If that string vibrates at 20 Hz. v?

questions.q: That string wave (λ = 2.0 m) vibrates at 20 Hz. What is its speed?
why: v = fλ.
questions.label: 37. That string wave (λ = 2.0 m) vibrates at 20 Hz. What is its speed?
questions.tip: Always write the formula before substituting.

similar.q: Can you hear 30 kHz?

questions.q: Can a person hear a sound of 30 kHz?
why: The human hearing range is about 20 Hz to 20 kHz.
30 kHz is above 20 kHz – ultrasound.
So people usually cannot hear it, but dogs and bats can.
questions.label: 38. Can a person hear a sound of 30 kHz?
questions.tip: Above 20 kHz = ultrasound; below 20 Hz = infrasound.

similar.q: Can EM radio 1 MHz be heard directly by the ear?
similar.a: No. Ear needs a mechanical sound wave.

questions.q: Can a 1 MHz radio wave be heard directly by the ear?
questions.answer: No. Ear needs a mechanical sound wave.
why: The ear detects mechanical vibrations of air (sound) between 20 Hz and 20 kHz.
A radio wave is an electromagnetic wave, not a vibration of air.
So it cannot be heard directly – a radio must convert it into sound.
questions.label: 39. Can a 1 MHz radio wave be heard directly by the ear?
questions.tip: Radio waves ≠ sound waves.

similar.q: What does a wave transfer, and what does it not transfer?
similar.a: Energy, not a net flow of the medium.

questions.q: What does a wave transfer, and what does it not transfer?
questions.answer: Energy, not a net flow of the medium.
why: A wave carries energy from the source to elsewhere.
The particles of the medium only vibrate about fixed positions.
So a wave transfers energy, not matter.
questions.label: 40. What does a wave transfer, and what does it not transfer?
questions.tip: Energy moves, matter stays.

similar.q: Two thin lenses of +2.5 D and −0.5 D are in contact. Find the combined power and focal length.
similar.a: P=2.0 D. f=0.50 m convex combination.

questions.q: Two thin lenses of +2.5 D and −0.5 D are in contact. Find the combined power and focal length.
questions.answer: P=2.0 D. f=0.50 m convex combination.
why: Lenses in contact: P = P₁ + P₂ = +2.5 D + (−0.5 D).
f = 1/P = 1/2.0 = 0.50 m – the combination is converging.
questions.label: 12. Two thin lenses of +2.5 D and −0.5 D are in contact. Find the combined power and focal length.
questions.tip: Positive total power → acts as a convex lens.

similar.q: f=512 Hz. Period?

questions.q: A tuning fork has f = 512 Hz. What is the period?
why: T ≈ 1.95 × 10⁻³ s (about 2 ms).
questions.label: 26. A tuning fork has f = 512 Hz. What is the period?
questions.tip: Period and frequency are reciprocals.

similar.q: Sound 340 m/s, f=680 Hz. Wavelength?

questions.q: Sound travels at 340 m/s with f = 680 Hz. What is its wavelength?
why: λ = v/f.
questions.label: 27. Sound travels at 340 m/s with f = 680 Hz. What is its wavelength?

similar.q: The same 680 Hz note travels in water (v = 1500 m/s). Find the new λ.
similar.a: λ=1500/680=2.21 m. Frequency stays with the source.

questions.q: The same 680 Hz note travels in water (v = 1500 m/s). Find the new λ.
questions.answer: λ=1500/680=2.21 m. Frequency stays with the source.
why: The frequency stays 680 Hz (set by the source).
questions.label: 28. The same 680 Hz note travels in water (v = 1500 m/s). Find the new λ.
questions.tip: Faster medium → longer wavelength.

similar.q: Echo from a wall returns in 0.50 s. d? (v=340)

questions.q: An echo from a wall returns in 0.50 s (v = 340 m/s). How far away is the wall?
why: d = vt/2.
questions.label: 29. An echo from a wall returns in 0.50 s (v = 340 m/s). How far away is the wall?
questions.tip: Echo time is the round trip.

similar.q: You stand 170 m from a cliff. Echo time?

questions.q: You stand 170 m from a cliff (v = 340 m/s). How long until you hear the echo?
why: The sound travels 2 × 170 = 340 m.
questions.label: 30. You stand 170 m from a cliff (v = 340 m/s). How long until you hear the echo?
questions.tip: t = 2d/v for echoes.

similar.q: Radio wave λ=150 m. Frequency?

questions.q: Radio wave λ=150 m. Frequency?
why: f = c/λ.
questions.label: 31. Radio wave λ=150 m. Frequency?
questions.tip: AM radio wavelengths are hundreds of metres.

similar.q: Double the amplitude of a sound wave. Pitch?

questions.q: The amplitude of a sound wave is doubled. What happens to its pitch?
why: Pitch depends only on frequency.
Doubling the amplitude does not change the frequency.
So the pitch is unchanged; the sound is louder (energy ×4).
questions.label: 33. The amplitude of a sound wave is doubled. What happens to its pitch?
questions.tip: Amplitude → loudness only.

similar.q: Why no sound on the Moon’s surface from a distant hammer?
similar.a: Vacuum — longitudinal sound has no medium. You would still see the hammer (EM).

questions.q: Why can't you hear a hammer striking a rock in the distance on the Moon's surface?
questions.answer: Vacuum — longitudinal sound has no medium. You would still see the hammer (EM).
why: The Moon has no atmosphere – near vacuum.
Sound is a mechanical (longitudinal) wave and needs a medium.
So no sound reaches you; you would still see the hammer because light (EM) crosses a vacuum.
questions.label: 34. Why can't you hear a hammer striking a rock in the distance on the Moon's surface?
questions.tip: Astronauts talk by radio.

similar.q: Put in order of increasing frequency: UV, radio, green light, X-rays.

questions.q: Put in order of increasing frequency: UV, radio, green light, X-rays.
why: Frequency increases from radio to gamma.
Of these: radio (lowest), green light, then UV.
X-rays highest: radio → green → UV → X-rays.
questions.label: 35. Put in order of increasing frequency: UV, radio, green light, X-rays.
questions.tip: Visible light sits between IR and UV.

similar.q: What is the phase relation between two points 3λ/2 apart on a travelling wave?

questions.q: What is the phase relation between two points 3λ/2 apart on a travelling wave?
why: λ/2 apart → antiphase; λ apart → in phase.
3λ/2 = λ + λ/2 – one full cycle plus half a cycle.
So the points are in opposite phase.
questions.label: 36. What is the phase relation between two points 3λ/2 apart on a travelling wave?
questions.tip: Odd multiples of λ/2 → antiphase.

similar.q: A string wave: 4 crests pass in 2.0 s. f?

questions.q: Four crests of a string wave pass a point in 2.0 s. What is the frequency?
why: Each crest is one cycle passing the point.
f = 4 cycles ÷ 2.0 s.
questions.label: 37. Four crests of a string wave pass a point in 2.0 s. What is the frequency?
questions.tip: f = number of cycles ÷ time.

similar.q: Those crests are 0.80 m apart. v?

questions.q: Those crests (f = 2.0 Hz) are 0.80 m apart. What is the wave speed?
why: Crest-to-crest distance = λ = 0.80 m.
questions.label: 38. Those crests (f = 2.0 Hz) are 0.80 m apart. What is the wave speed?
questions.tip: Neighbouring crests are one wavelength apart.

similar.q: Using v = fλ: in the same medium, if f is doubled, what happens to λ?  A) ×2  B) Unchanged  C) Halves  D) Becomes c

questions.q: Using v = fλ: in the same medium, if f is doubled, what happens to λ?
why: In the same medium v stays constant.
v = fλ, so λ = v/f.
Doubling f halves λ – answer C.
questions.tip: f and λ are inversely proportional at fixed v.

similar.q: What happens to sound in a vacuum?  A) Travels at c  B) Speeds up  C) Becomes radio  D) It cannot travel (no medium)

questions.q: What happens to sound in a vacuum?
why: Sound is a mechanical wave carried by particles.
A vacuum contains no particles.
So sound cannot travel in a vacuum – answer D.
questions.tip: Only EM waves travel through a vacuum.
